newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australians say Indonesia not to blame for Bre-X.
newsitem.headline: Australians say Indonesia not to blame for Bre-X.

text.p: Shocked Australian gold mining companies with operations in Indonesia said on Monday the Bre-X Minerals Ltd Busang gold scandal was a Canadian not an Indonesian problem.
"It's quite shocking," John Quinn, managing director and chief executive officer of Newcrest Mining Ltd, said.
Newcrest last week announced that it was starting several gold ventures in Indonesia.

The company said it had signed three contract cover applications over ground in Halmahera, East Sumbawa and West Sunmatra, in Indonesia. It has had a contract of work over a prospect in North Sulawesi.

One Australian analyst on Monday, commenting on the Bre-X scandal, singled out Newcrest as an example of how Australian gold explorers might now find it "tough" to achieve gains from Indonesian operations.
"Well, it shouldn't," Newcrest's Quinn said.

"Frankly if somebody suggests that we conducted oursevlves in the way that Strathcona have now suggested certain people associated with Busang have, then they might be on the sharp end of a bit of litigation," he said.
"It's not an Indonesia problem. (So) why should it reflect on one of Newcrest's assets, simply because it's in Indonesia? The logic does not stand up," he said.
Quinn went on to say that Busang was a Canadian problem.
"(But) it could have happened in any country of Latin America, it could theoretically happen in Australia,...Africa, it could happen in any number of places," he said.
"The fact that it was in Indonesia is more happenchance than anything else. There is nothing unique about Indonesia that may it more or less susceptible to this.
"This is a Canadian company with Canadian management that was involved. It was not an Indonesian company at all," he said.
Other international companies with gold ventures in Indonesia had not encountered Bre-X-style problems, he said.
With regulatory requirements much more stringent in Australia than in Canada, the main impact would show through in the need for a tightening of Canadian regulations, he said.
Ian Burston, managing director and cheief executive of Aurora Gold Ltd, said Aurora was an established gold producer in Indonesia.
This raised hopes that the market would exercise discretion between producers/developers compared with explorers.
"Whether that will be the case in what happens I don't know. But from our perspective it's business as usual," he said.
Aurora has mining operations in Indonesia's Kalimantan and has new areas in north Sulawesi.
"We're quite confident about going ahead and getting on with our business," he said. "I guess that will sort itself out...pretty startling stuff isn't it?"
Indonesian authorities would now focus on their regulations, as would the Canadians, he said.
Other Australian companies with gold mining ventures in Indonesia include Laverton Gold NL, in Sumatra.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
